nameStory: Caraway gets its name from the Arabic 'karawya,' which traveled through Latin and French before reaching English. This ancient spice has been seasoning our food for thousands of years, and its name reflects its long journey from the Middle East to European gardens and eventually to New England.
description: Caraway is a delicate-looking biennial herb that reaches 1-2 feet tall, belonging to the carrot family. In its first year, it forms a low rosette of feathery, finely-divided leaves that look almost fern-like. During its second year, it sends up slender stems topped with small white flower clusters that eventually produce the aromatic seeds we know as the caraway spice.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, thread-like leaflets that are finely divided two or three times, creating a delicate, lacy appearance similar to carrot tops but more finely cut. Crush a leaf between your fingers for a distinctive spicy-sweet aroma.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers arranged in flat-topped umbrella-like clusters (umbels) about 2-4 inches across, typical of the carrot family. Each individual flower is only about 1/8 inch across with 5 small white petals.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, curved, brown seeds about 1/4 inch long with distinctive ridges running lengthwise. When crushed, they release the familiar warm, slightly sweet and spicy caraway scent used in rye bread.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a low rosette of leaves in the first year, then sends up branching flower stems in the second year. The whole plant has a delicate, wispy appearance even when fully grown.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Slender, hollow, and ridged stems that are smooth to the touch and often have a slight purple tinge. The stems branch near the top to support multiple flower clusters.

habitat: Look for caraway in disturbed soils, old gardens, roadsides, and waste places throughout New England. It prefers sunny locations with well-drained soil and often appears near old homesteads or in areas where it has escaped from cultivation. You might find it growing alongside other members of the carrot family like Queen Anne's lace.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants show their feathery rosettes of leaves emerging from the ground. Second-year plants begin sending up their flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs from June through August, with the characteristic white umbrella-shaped flower clusters most visible in early to mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and turn brown, becoming aromatic when crushed. The plant begins to die back after releasing its seeds.
seasonality.winter: First-year rosettes may persist under snow, while second-year plants have completed their life cycle and died back completely.

funFact: Caraway seeds aren't actually seeds at all – they're technically fruits called schizocarps that split in half when ripe, and each 'seed' you see in your spice rack is actually half of the original fruit containing one true seed inside!
confusionNotes: Caraway is easily confused with other carrot family members like wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace) and poison hemlock. The key difference is caraway's much more finely divided, thread-like leaves and its distinctive spicy-sweet smell when crushed – Queen Anne's lace smells more carrot-like, while poison hemlock has a musty, unpleasant odor.
contextualKnowledge: While caraway the spice is familiar to most people from rye bread and European cooking, many don't realize it can be found growing wild in New England. The plant escaped from colonial herb gardens and still occasionally pops up in the landscape, though it's much less common than other carrot family members.
compareHints: Caraway is the only member of its genus (Carum) commonly found in New England. Among other carrot family members, it's distinguished by having the most finely divided leaves – even more delicate than dill or fennel – and by its characteristic spicy-sweet fragrance that's immediately recognizable to anyone familiar with caraway seeds from baking.
